# R12 — Mutation Discipline (Encapsulated State)

## Principle

A validated value changes state only through methods that own its invariants — never
through leaked internals. Constructors copy the slices and maps they are given;
queries return copies (or iterators), not the internal reference; a method is a query
or a modifier, not both; and a type with a validating constructor exposes no setter
that skips the validation.

## Why

R2's payoff — validate once, trust the value everywhere after — is void the moment an
internal slice escapes. In Go, `return g.perms` does not return the permissions; it
returns a mutable alias into them. The caller can sort, truncate, or overwrite the
"validated" state without calling a single method. The same aliasing runs backward: a
constructor that stores a caller's slice without copying has handed its state to code
it has never met.

## Design guidance

- **Copy at both edges.** A constructor clones slice/map arguments (or builds fresh ones); a query returns `slices.Clone`/`maps.Clone` or an iterator.
- **Iterators beat copies for read paths.** When callers only range, expose `iter.Seq[T]` — no alias escapes and no copy is paid.
- **A method is a query or a modifier.** A caller who wants the value must be able to get it without causing the side effect.
- **No setters around a validating constructor.** A `SetPort(n)` that assigns without checking is a hole in ParsePort's wall. If post-construction change is a real requirement, the mutator validates exactly as the constructor does — or returns a new value.
- **One variable, one purpose.**
- **The inverse trap: ceremony copies.** Cloning a slice that never escapes the function is defensive noise.

## Fix pattern

- **Copy on the Way In**: constructor stores `slices.Clone(arg)`/`maps.Clone(arg)` instead of the caller's reference.
- **Copy on the Way Out / Encapsulate Collection**: queries on validated types return clones or iterators.
- **Separate Query from Modifier**.
- **Remove Setting Method**: delete the setter; route the change through a validating mutator, a WithX copy-constructor, or full reconstruction via ParseX.
- **Split Variable**.

# R10 — Concurrency Safety

## Principle

Every goroutine has an owner and a provable exit path; shared mutable state is owned
by one type and guarded where it lives; production code never sleeps to pace or
synchronize cancellable work. Concurrency is designed at construction time.

## Why

The race detector finds races only at runtime, only on paths a test happens to
exercise. A leaked goroutine accumulates silently; an unsynchronized concurrent map
write is a fatal runtime crash, not an error; a bare `time.Sleep` in a retry loop
holds a cancelled request hostage for the full backoff.

## Design guidance

- **Whoever starts a goroutine owns its shutdown.** Fire-and-forget goroutines are acceptable only in main-adjacent wiring that lives as long as the process.
- **Every blocking loop selects on its exit.** A `for` loop containing a channel receive/send/sleep gets a `select` with a `ctx.Done()` case.
- **State and its guard are one unit.** Shared mutable state lives on one type with the mutex declared directly above the fields it guards, and every access goes through that type's methods.
- **Prefer handing off to sharing.**
- **Pick the right guard.** A counter/flag can be an atomic instead of a mutex; sync.Map only for append-only/disjoint-key caches.
- **Production code does not sleep.** Backoff/pacing/polling are time.After/Ticker inside a select with ctx.Done(); sustained rate limiting uses x/time/rate.
- **The linter owns the mechanical neighbors** (errcheck, bodyclose, govet copylocks) — don't re-hunt those.

## Fix pattern

- **Inject the Exit Path**: add a ctx.Done() case to the goroutine's blocking loop; thread ctx from the caller.
- **Make the Goroutine Joinable**: return an owner with Wait/Close, or use errgroup.Group/sync.WaitGroup.
- **Extract Synchronized Owner**: move shared state plus its mutex onto one type; all access via methods. This proposes a new type — expect the over-abstraction skeptic to challenge it.
- **Replace Sleep with Timer Select**.
- **Delete Unearned Guards**: a mutex on state only one goroutine ever touches is ceremony.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does every goroutine started in the diff have a provable exit path?**
   Detection: `grep -nE '\bgo\s+[a-zA-Z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*\(|\.Go\(' <files>` — catches `go func(...)`, method values, `.Go(...)` spawns. For each hit, read the goroutine body: a `for` loop or blocking channel op must have a `ctx.Done()`/closed-channel `select` case.
   Violation: an unbounded loop or blocking send/receive with no exit case; a loop with a `default:` case spinning at 100% CPU is equally a violation.

2. **Can the code that starts a goroutine also stop it and wait for it?**
   Detection: check what the spawning function returns/exposes: a ctx it honors plus a Wait/Close/done-channel, or an errgroup/WaitGroup the caller holds.
   Violation: fire-and-forget in library code.

3. **Is shared mutable state written from a goroutine without a guard?**
   Detection: for each `go func`, list writes to captured variables, receiver fields, maps; cross-check guards (sync.Mutex, sync.Map, atomic, chan) or confinement to one goroutine.
   Violation: any write reachable from two goroutines with no mutex/channel ownership.

4. **Does each mutex live next to the data it guards, and is the lock taken on every access?**
   Detection: check guarded fields sit in the same struct; grep field names across the package for unlocked access paths.
   Violation: a mutex guarding fields it doesn't live beside, or any access path that skips the lock.

5. **Does production code sleep?**
   Detection: `grep -n 'time\.Sleep' <files> | grep -v _test.go`
   Violation: any hit on a cancellable path. Exempt: startup jitter in main-adjacent wiring.

6. **Inverse — is a guard or goroutine ceremony?**
   Detection: for each NEW mutex/goroutine, grep the package for a second goroutine that ever touches the guarded state, or a caller that needed the work to be async.
   Violation: a mutex on single-goroutine state, or a goroutine whose caller immediately blocks waiting for it.

# R11 — Conditional Dispatch (Anti-IF)

## Principle

A conditional that asks what a value *is* — a type switch, or a switch/if-chain on a
kind/status/mode discriminator — may exist ONCE. The second copy of that discriminator
is a missing polymorphic type: the variants want to be implementations of an interface
(or entries in a dispatch map), chosen once at the boundary. One well-placed,
exhaustive switch is not a defect; a duplicated one always is.

## Why

Every `if (new kind) { new code }` doubles the execution paths. Kind-switches
replicate: the same `switch msg.Channel` appears in send, validate, format, and retry
code, and adding a variant means finding and editing every copy — the one you miss is
the bug that ships. The compiler cannot help: an if-chain has no notion of
completeness. Dispatching once collapses N switches into one construction site.

## Design guidance

- **The trigger is duplication, not existence.** One site — keep the switch (make it exhaustive). Two or more — the variants are a type family; dispatch.
- **Decide once, at the edge.** The one legitimate inspection of the raw discriminator is the constructor/parser that picks the implementation. A type switch over an interface the same package owns is always a re-ask.
- **Dispatch requires owning the output.** An interface method can only be written in the package that declares the interface. When the switch's output format belongs to a consumer and the variants live in a shared API package, the move is unavailable — shrink to pure dispatch and stop.
- **Interface vs strategy map.** Variants with several behaviors/state → interface. Variants that differ by a single function → a map.
- **Null object over nil-checks.**
- **Flag arguments are two functions.** `func Render(a Alert, short bool)` → split into `Render`/`RenderShort`.
- **A kept switch must be exhaustive.** Name the enum, drop the default, let `exhaustive` linter prove completeness.
- **The over-abstraction trap, dispatch edition.** An interface with one production implementation is R6's territory; two trivial implementations behind one switch at one site score LOW on R1's juiciness scorecard — keep the conditional.

## Fix pattern

- **Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch**: define the interface from the union of what all copies do; one type per variant; introduce ParseX as the single decision point.
- **Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map**: single-behavior variance → package-level map[Kind]func(...).
- **Introduce Null Object**.
- **Split Flag Argument**.
- **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**: one site, closed enum → named enum type, no default, exhaustive linter enforcing completeness.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Is the same discriminator inspected in more than one place?**
   Detection: list discriminators — `grep -nE 'switch [a-zA-Z_.]+\.(Type|Kind|Status|Mode|Channel|Format|Level)\b'` and if-chain forms `grep -nE 'if [a-zA-Z_.]+\.(Type|Kind|Status|Mode|Channel|Format|Level) =='`; then count each across the package.
   Violation: ≥2 sites inspecting one discriminator — the decision has no single owner.

2. **Does a type switch dispatch on concrete types outside a boundary?**
   Detection: `grep -rn 'switch .* := .*\.(type)' --include='*.go' .` — is it in a ParseX/decoder/boundary adapter, or in business logic?
   Violation: a type switch in domain logic whose cases call variant-specific behavior. A switch over an interface the SAME package owns is a violation even at a single site.

3. **Does a `default:` (or trailing `else`) handle "unknown kind" away from the boundary?**
   Detection: for each switch found in Q1, check the default arm for errors.New/fmt.Errorf/panic on an unknown-kind message.
   Violation: unknown-kind errors deep in the call graph.

4. **Does a boolean parameter select between behaviors?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'func .*\(.*\b(is|use|with|enable|skip)[A-Za-z]* bool'`; check whether the function branches on it near the top.
   Violation: a flag argument whose branches share little code.

5. **Inverse — is a NEW dispatch abstraction unearned?**
   Detection: for each new interface/strategy map, count production implementations/entries and the number of sites the old conditional occupied.
   Violation: one switching site with trivial variance replaced by an interface — score it; if LOW, the fix is Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch.

# R12 — Mutation Discipline (Encapsulated State)

## Principle

A validated value changes state only through methods that own its invariants — never
through leaked internals. Constructors copy the slices and maps they are given;
queries return copies (or iterators), not the internal reference; a method is a query
or a modifier, not both; and a type with a validating constructor exposes no setter
that skips the validation.

## Why

R2's payoff — validate once, trust the value everywhere after — is void the moment an
internal slice escapes. In Go, `return g.perms` does not return the permissions; it
returns a mutable alias into them. The caller can sort, truncate, or overwrite the
"validated" state without calling a single method. The same aliasing runs backward: a
constructor that stores a caller's slice without copying has handed its state to code
it has never met.

## Design guidance

- **Copy at both edges.** A constructor clones slice/map arguments (or builds fresh ones); a query returns `slices.Clone`/`maps.Clone` or an iterator.
- **Iterators beat copies for read paths.** When callers only range, expose `iter.Seq[T]` — no alias escapes and no copy is paid.
- **A method is a query or a modifier.** A caller who wants the value must be able to get it without causing the side effect.
- **No setters around a validating constructor.** A `SetPort(n)` that assigns without checking is a hole in ParsePort's wall. If post-construction change is a real requirement, the mutator validates exactly as the constructor does — or returns a new value.
- **One variable, one purpose.**
- **The inverse trap: ceremony copies.** Cloning a slice that never escapes the function is defensive noise.

## Fix pattern

- **Copy on the Way In**: constructor stores `slices.Clone(arg)`/`maps.Clone(arg)` instead of the caller's reference.
- **Copy on the Way Out / Encapsulate Collection**: queries on validated types return clones or iterators.
- **Separate Query from Modifier**.
- **Remove Setting Method**: delete the setter; route the change through a validating mutator, a WithX copy-constructor, or full reconstruction via ParseX.
- **Split Variable**.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does a method return an internal slice or map by reference?**
   Detection: for each type with a validating constructor, list its slice/map fields, then grep for a bare `return x.field` with no Clone/copy/iterator around it.
   Violation: an internal reference escapes a validated type — Copy on the Way Out.

2. **Does a constructor store a caller-provided slice/map without copying?**
   Detection: inside each ParseX/NewX, check the struct literal for a slice/map field assigned directly from a parameter identifier.
   Violation: the type's state aliases memory the caller still holds. (A collection built inside the constructor is fine.)

3. **Does one method both return domain data and mutate the receiver?**
   Detection: for each method with a non-error return value, grep its body for assignments to receiver fields (`<recv>.<field> =`, `append(<recv>.`).
   Violation: a query/modifier hybrid where any call site discards the return value or calls it only for the effect.

4. **Can a validated type be mutated around its constructor?**
   Detection: grep for setters (`func (recv *Type) SetX`); for each hit, does the receiver type have a ParseX/NewX that validates, and does the setter re-check?
   Violation: a setter that assigns unchecked on a constructor-validated type.

5. **Is one variable reassigned to mean something different?**
   Detection: read each function; for every reassignment, ask whether the right-hand side computes the same concept.
   Violation: two meanings under one name.

6. **Inverse — does the diff copy defensively where no alias escapes?**
   Detection: for each Clone/copy loop, trace the copied value: does it ever cross a function boundary or outlive the call?
   Violation: cloning data that provably never escapes — ceremony.
=====

## R10 — Concurrency Safety: Findings

**Confirmed via `.golangci.yaml`:** `govet` has only `copylocks` enabled; `bodyclose` is NOT enabled (irrelevant to R10 anyway). Per rule, `copylocks` is a mechanical neighbor — I did not re-report the `Cache.String()`/`describe(*c)` value-copy-of-a-mutex itself (cache.go:83,86), only the *distinct* unlocked-read issue it exposes.

---

```
R10 | internal/services/device_service.go:103,568-578 | Q1: `go s.flushLoop()` spawns a goroutine whose body (`for { time.Sleep(50*time.Millisecond); ... }`, lines 569-577) is an unbounded `for` loop with no `select`/`ctx.Done()` case — it can never exit. Q2: `Close()` (lines 559-564) only clears `s.cache`, it never signals flushLoop to stop, so the goroutine outlives every DeviceService that is closed. | Inject the Exit Path + Make the Goroutine Joinable | M
```

```
R10 | internal/services/device_service.go:218,463-467,572-576 | Q3/Q4: `s.lastSeen` map is written/deleted from three places with inconsistent locking: ProcessHeartbeat `s.lastSeen[id] = d.LastSeen` (line 218) — no lock, despite comment "bounds-checked: map access never panics" (false for concurrent writes); Purge's second loop (lines 463-467) deletes from `s.lastSeen` *after* `s.mu.Unlock()` at line 462; flushLoop (lines 572-576, running in its own goroutine per finding above) iterates+deletes `s.lastSeen` with zero locking. Meanwhile `Flush()` (line 548) reads the same map correctly under `s.mu`. Two+ goroutines (request handlers and flushLoop) can race on this map → classic "fatal error: concurrent map writes" per the rule's own rationale. | Extract Synchronized Owner | M
```

```
R10 | internal/services/cache.go:28-34 | Q4: `Put` locks `c.mu` only for `c.items[key] = d` (line 31) then unlocks (line 32) before writing `c.ttl[key] = time.Now().Add(c.span)` at line 33 — that write to `c.ttl` races with `Get`'s locked iteration/write of the same map (lines 42-51). | Extract Synchronized Owner | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/cache.go:56-58 | Q4: `func (c *Cache) All() map[string]models.Device { return c.items }` takes no lock at all and hands back the live map reference — any concurrent `Put`/`Get` (which do lock and mutate `c.items`) races with a caller ranging/reading the returned map. | Extract Synchronized Owner | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/cache.go:82-88 | Q4: `String()`→`describe(*c)` reads `len(c.items)`/`len(c.ttl)` with no lock held (distinct from the govet-copylocks value-copy issue, which is the linter's mechanical-neighbor territory and not re-hunted here) — a concurrent `Put`/`Get` can mutate the same underlying maps while this reads them. | Extract Synchronized Owner | S
```

```
R10 | internal/jobs/scheduler.go:54 | Q1: `for _, job := range s.drain() { if ctx.Err() != nil { return }; ...; ch <- pool.Job{...} }` — the blocking channel send `ch <- pool.Job{...}` has no `select` with a `ctx.Done()` case. If the buffered `ch` (size `env.Config.BatchSize`) is full and the worker pool stalls, a cancelled `ctx` cannot unblock this send. | Inject the Exit Path | S
```

```
R10 | internal/pool/workers.go:17-21 | Q2: `Start(jobs <-chan Job)` spawns `env.Config.NumWorkers` goroutines (`go worker(jobs)`, line 19) and returns nothing — no WaitGroup, no handle. This is library code (`internal/pool`), not main-adjacent process wiring, so the caller (`scheduler.Run`, scheduler.go:45) can close the channel but has no way to wait for the worker goroutines themselves to actually return. | Make the Goroutine Joinable | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/device_service.go:181 | Q5: `time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond)` inside the `retry:`/`goto` loop of `ProcessHeartbeat`, which is called directly from the heartbeat HTTP handler (internal/handlers/heartbeat.go:38). `ProcessHeartbeat` takes no `ctx` at all, so up to 3 attempts (≈0-600ms) of sleeping block the request goroutine with no cancellation path. | Replace Sleep with Timer Select | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/device_service.go:486 and internal/services/retry.go:34-43 | Q5: `DeviceService.Retry(ctx context.Context, ...)` accepts a `ctx` (device_service.go:475) but calls `withRetry(3, func() error {...})` (line 486), and `withRetry` (retry.go:34-43) sleeps via plain `time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * time.Second)` (line 40) with no `ctx` parameter at all — cancelling the caller's context cannot interrupt up to 6s of backoff. | Replace Sleep with Timer Select | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/retry.go:46-55 | Q5: `SendWithRetry(a models.Alert, p models.Priority)` has no `ctx` parameter and sleeps via `time.Sleep(retryDelay(a))` (line 52) inside its retry loop — any future caller on a cancellable path has no way to abort the backoff. | Replace Sleep with Timer Select | S
```

```
R10 | internal/services/sync_service.go:122 | Q5: `SyncService.Run(ctx context.Context)` (line 41) receives a ctx, but `syncOne`→`saveWithRetry` (lines 82-126) drops it — `saveWithRetry` calls `s.repo.Save(context.TODO(), d)` (line 118) and sleeps via `time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 100 * time.Millisecond)` (line 122) with no reference to the caller's ctx, so a cancelled sync run cannot abort mid-retry. | Replace Sleep with Timer Select | S
```

**Checked clean (no finding):**
- `cmd/svc/main.go:29` `time.Sleep(time.Duration(rand.IntN(20)) * time.Millisecond)` — startup jitter in main-adjacent wiring, explicitly exempted by the rule; comment at lines 27-28 documents the reason.
- `cmd/svc/main.go:55` `go scheduler.Run(ctx)` — main-adjacent wiring; `Run` honors `ctx.Err()` in its drain loop and `Scheduler.Wait()` exists, satisfying the main-adjacent exemption (the internal channel-send gap is reported separately above).
- `internal/repository/mem_store.go` — `Get`/`Save`/`List` all lock `mu` consistently around `devices`.
- `internal/repository/file_repo.go` — `Get`/`Save`/`List` all lock `mu` consistently.
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go` mutex — `Enqueue`/`drain`/`record`/`Completed`/`Failed` all lock consistently around `pending`/`completed`/`failed`; `wg` used correctly via `Add`/`Done`/`Wait`.
- `internal/services/snapshot_service.go` — `taken` is consistently locked in `take`/`Taken`/`Manifest`; `lastRun` is unguarded but not reachable from two goroutines anywhere in the current call graph (service is only instantiated in tests) — no evidence of a violation.
- `internal/mocks/repo.go` — `Get`/`Save`/`List`/`count` all lock consistently; test double, no violation.
- `internal/services/device_service.go` `AuditLog` (lines 21-55) — `Write`/`Count` lock consistently.

`R10: 11 findings — hunted across internal/ and cmd/ non-test .go files; goroutine-spawn, mutex, and time.Sleep detection commands run over the full scope.`

## R12 — Mutation Discipline (Encapsulated State) — Findings

**Finding 1 — Q1: bare slice return, canonical case**
`internal/models/grants.go:24`
```go
func (g Grants) All() []Permission {
	return g.perms
}
```
`Grants` has a constructor (`NewGrants`, line 18) and `perms []Permission` is a slice field (line 14). `All()` returns the field directly with no `slices.Clone`. A caller can `g.All()[0] = ...` or sort/truncate the slice, silently corrupting the value everywhere it's shared.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out** (or **Encapsulate Collection** with an `iter.Seq[Permission]`).
Effort: S

**Finding 2 — Q2: constructor stores caller's slice unclonad**
`internal/models/grants.go:18-19`
```go
func NewGrants(perms ...Permission) Grants {
	return Grants{perms: perms}
}
```
The struct literal assigns the field directly from the parameter identifier `perms` with no clone. If called as `NewGrants(existingSlice...)`, the variadic parameter aliases the caller's backing array (Go passes the slice through unmodified when spread with `...`), so `Grants` state can be mutated by the caller after construction.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way In** (`Grants{perms: slices.Clone(perms)}`).
Effort: S

**Finding 3 — Q1: bare slice return**
`internal/models/schedule.go:32-34`
```go
func (s Schedule) Days() []Weekday {
	return s.days
}
```
`Schedule` has a validating constructor `NewSchedule` (line 19, rejects empty/invalid weekdays) and `days []Weekday` is a slice field (line 15). `Days()` leaks the internal slice with no clone — a caller can reorder/truncate the validated day-set.
Contrast: `internal/snapshot/schedule.go:87-89` does this correctly — `func (p Plan) Windows() []Window { return slices.Clone(p.windows) }` — confirming the fix is known and used elsewhere in this codebase, just missed here.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out**.
Effort: S

**Finding 4 — Q2: constructor stores caller's slice unclonad**
`internal/models/schedule.go:19-28`
```go
func NewSchedule(days []Weekday) (Schedule, error) {
	...
	return Schedule{days: days}, nil
}
```
`days` (the parameter) is validated element-by-element but stored by direct assignment — no `slices.Clone(days)`. The caller's original slice is still held by the caller, who can mutate it after the fact, changing the "validated" `Schedule`'s contents post-construction without any Schedule method being called.
Contrast: `internal/snapshot/schedule.go:73-78` does the equivalent correctly (`Plan{windows: slices.Clone(windows)}`, with a comment explicitly calling out why).
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way In**.
Effort: S

**Finding 5 — Q1: internal slice element leaked via pointer**
`internal/report/catalog.go:27-34`
```go
func (c *Catalog) Find(name string) *Device {
	for i := range c.devices {
		if c.devices[i].Name == name {
			return &c.devices[i]
		}
	}
	return nil
}
```
`Catalog` has a validating/copying constructor `NewCatalog` (line 22, correctly does `slices.Clone(devices)` — confirmed clean for Q2). But `Find` hands back `&c.devices[i]`, a live pointer into the catalog's internal backing array. Any caller can do `cat.Find("x").Name = "y"` and mutate the catalog's stored state directly — worse than a slice-return alias, since it's a pointer to a specific internal element, no copy involved at all. Current caller (`internal/report/wire.go:10-11`) only reads via the pointer today, but the API shape itself is the violation — nothing stops a future/other caller from writing through it.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out** (return `(Device, bool)` by value, or `int, bool` index if identity is needed).
Effort: S

**Finding 6 — Q1: bare map return**
`internal/services/cache.go:56-58`
```go
func (c *Cache) All() map[string]models.Device {
	return c.items
}
```
`items map[string]models.Device` is guarded by `c.mu` everywhere else (`Put`, `Get`, `Len`, `Footprint` all lock). `All()` returns the live map with **no lock taken and no `maps.Clone`** — the caller gets a direct alias to the cache's internal map and can read/write it concurrently with `Put`/`Get`, both racing on the map and bypassing every invariant the mutex is meant to protect.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out** (`maps.Clone(c.items)` under lock, or expose an `iter.Seq2[string, models.Device]`).
Effort: S

**Finding 7 — Q1 (borderline): mutex-protected slice escapes by reference**
`internal/services/snapshot_service.go:88-92` and `:107-116`
```go
func (s *SnapshotService) Taken() []models.Snapshot {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	return s.taken
}
...
func (s *SnapshotService) Manifest() map[string]interface{} {
	...
	return map[string]interface{}{
		...
		"snapshots": s.taken,
	}
}
```
`s.taken` is appended to under `s.mu` in `take()` (line 81), establishing an invariant that all mutation is lock-protected. Both `Taken()` and `Manifest()` release the lock while still holding/exposing the same backing slice reference (`Manifest` nests it inside a returned map), so a caller ranging over the returned slice/map value races with a concurrent `take()` append, and can mutate elements directly. `SnapshotService` doesn't have a validating `ParseX`/`NewX` in the strict sense the rule's Q1 detection targets, so this is weaker than Findings 1/3, but the aliasing mechanics and invariant-escape are identical to the canonical case.
Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out** (`slices.Clone(s.taken)` before returning/embedding).
Effort: S

---

**Investigated, not findings:**
- `internal/models/heartbeat.go:21` `return h.Raw` — `Raw` is a `string` (immutable in Go); no aliasing possible. Excluded (Q1 doesn't apply).
- `internal/models/device.go:16-19` `SetStatus` — `Device` has **no** `ParseX`/`NewX` validating constructor anywhere in the repo (confirmed via grep: it's always built with plain struct literals in `handlers/devices.go:36`, `services/device_service.go:159,338`, tests, etc.). Status validation (`validateDevice`, `models.IsValidStatus`) lives at the service layer, not on the type. Q4's criterion ("does the receiver type have a ParseX/NewX that validates") is not met, so this does not qualify as an R12 violation under this rule's falsifying question — excluded.
- `internal/services/cache.go:38-53` `Get` (refresh-expiry-and-fetch) — atomic get+expire is explicitly documented (`// Get returns the cached device and refreshes its expiry...`), and both call sites (`internal/services/service_test.go:75,79`) consume the boolean result meaningfully, not calling it only for the mutating side effect. Falls under the rule's own carve-out ("if every caller genuinely needs both halves atomically... it is one operation"). Not a Q3 violation.
- `internal/services/device_service.go:223-239` `Get` (cache-hit counters + return) — mutates `s.hits`/`s.misses` telemetry counters alongside the return, but these aren't part of any validated collection/invariant being leaked; excluded from Q3.
- `internal/snapshot/schedule.go` `NewPlan`/`Windows()` — confirmed clean: constructor clones on the way in (line 77 `slices.Clone(windows)`), query clones on the way out (line 88 `slices.Clone(p.windows)`). Used as the contrast example above.
- `internal/services/device_service.go` `List`/`Export`/`Health`/`Stats`/`Flush` — all build fresh slices/maps or copy-loop before returning (e.g. `Stats()` line 522-539, `Health()` line 500-505); no bare internal-field aliasing found.
- `internal/report/catalog.go` `NewCatalog` — clean, clones on the way in (Q2 satisfied correctly).
- `internal/models/tenant.go`, `region.go`, `priority.go` — string/int-backed value types, no slice/map fields, no aliasing surface.
- `internal/jobs/scheduler.go` `Completed()`/`Failed()` — `int` fields, not slice/map; excluded.

`R12: 7 findings (grants.go x2, schedule.go x2, catalog.go x1, cache.go x1, snapshot_service.go x1); 12 leads/areas checked (grants.go, models/schedule.go, snapshot/schedule.go, heartbeat.go, cache.go, catalog.go, device.go SetStatus, device_service.go List/Export/Health/Stats/Flush, snapshot_service.go, alert_service.go, sync_service.go, jobs/scheduler.go, placement/picker.go, region.go, priority.go, tenant.go), detection commands (grep for bare `return x.field`, setter scan, constructor struct-literal scan) run across full internal/ and cmd/ scope.`

1	# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper
2	
3	Demonstrates: R1
4	
5	A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
6	cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
7	correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.
8	
9	## The setting
10	
11	During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
12	lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
13	two booleans tracked related state:
14	
15	```go
16	var (
17	    isClusterCIDRSet bool
18	    isServerCIDRSet  bool
19	)
20	// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
21	if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
22	    return // both set, nothing to do
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
27	travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
28	step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.
29	
30	## The extraction that was tried
31	
32	```go
33	// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
34	type CIDRPresence bool
35	
36	const (
37	    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
38	)
39	
40	func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
41	    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
42	}
43	
44	type CIDRConfig struct {
45	    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
46	    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
47	}
48	
49	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
50	    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Why it was rejected
55	
56	1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
57	2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
58	3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
59	   unrepresentable.
60	4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
61	   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
62	   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
63	5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
64	   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
65	6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.
66	
67	The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
68	mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
69	type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
70	need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.
71	
72	## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
73	
74	When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:
75	
76	```go
77	type CIDRConfig struct {
78	    ClusterCIDRSet bool
79	    ServiceCIDRSet bool
80	}
81	```
82	
83	`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
84	zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
85	surface; short-lived value).
86	
87	## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
88	
89	When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
90	with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
91	
92	```go
93	// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
94	// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
95	type CIDRConfig struct {

# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
two booleans tracked related state:

```go
var (
    isClusterCIDRSet bool
    isServerCIDRSet  bool
)
// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
    return // both set, nothing to do
}
```

Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
type CIDRPresence bool

const (
    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
)

func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
}

type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
   unrepresentable.
4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.

The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming

When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:

```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDRSet bool
    ServiceCIDRSet bool
}
```

`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
surface; short-lived value).

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)

When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:

```go
// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
}
```

Why this beat the wrapper:

- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.

## The decision, tabulated

| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:

1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
   wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**

Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

1	# Comment Noise Case: Nine Private Helpers, Nine Comments
2	
3	Demonstrates: R9 (comment policy — the visibility default)
4	
5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an
6	LLM flow before the visibility default existed. It detects which codec decoded a
7	reply body: JSON, or the client's configured non-JSON codec (msgpack). Every one
8	of its nine unexported symbols carries a comment; the file has more comment lines
9	than code lines. Each comment, judged alone, "delivers a toolbox value". The file
10	as a whole is unreadable — a human reviewer of a sibling PR called the style
11	"utterly lacking empathy for the reader".
12	
13	This is the case law for R9's visibility default: **unexported symbols get no
14	comment; the special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.**
15	
16	## The before — representative excerpts
17	
18	A 5-line comment on a private constant, with cross-repo provenance:
19	
20	```go
21	// nonJSONLeadingByteFloor is the lowest leading byte a non-JSON wire
22	// frame can start with in the leading-byte detection heuristic:
23	// JSON-RPC 2.0 envelopes always start with '{' (0x7b), and msgpack maps
24	// (fixmap, map16, map32) always start at 0x80 or above — the same
25	// boundary the legacy client's detectCodec uses.
26	nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
27	```
28	
29	Decoder rings and review-defense narration on another constant:
30	
31	```go
32	// msgpackAliasContentType is the second literal spelling D-04 requires
33	// this package to accept as msgpack, alongside jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack
34	// ("application/msgpack"). Named as a single constant — not a table —
35	// per Pitfall 3: a third wire format would earn its own narrow check,
36	// not a generalized alias registry.
37	msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
38	```
39	
40	Six lines on a one-line function, with forward references to its callers:
41	
42	```go
43	// trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data unchanged
44	// when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's byte verdict
45	// (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode it
46	// (Client.ParseResponse): encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading
47	// byte rather than whitespace, so leaving it in would still fail to decode
48	// even after correct classification.
49	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
50	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
51	}
52	```
53	
54	A caller list that rots on the next caller:
55	
56	```go
57	// normalizeContentType strips any ";"-delimited parameters (e.g.
58	// "; charset=binary"), trims surrounding whitespace, and lowercases the
59	// result — the shared normalization step both isMsgpackAliasContentType and
60	// replyCodecAndMismatch's header cross-check use (see codec_event.go).
61	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
62	```
63	
64	And the centerpiece: **22 prose lines on an unexported function** — over 4× the
65	budget of an exported crossroads — ending in a sixty-word sentence:
66	
67	```go
68	// replyCodecAndMismatch returns the byte-verdict codec (identical to
69	// detectReplyCodec) plus a bool that is true when the normalized
70	// Content-Type header disagrees with that byte verdict. The byte verdict
71	// always governs the actual decode (D-04: bytes-first); mismatch is only a
72	// signal for the caller's CodecEvent, never a second decode selector.
73	//
74	// headerSaysNonJSON is true when the header exactly names nonJSON's own
75	// content type, OR — the msgpack-alias carve-out D-04 requires — the
76	// header is either msgpack spelling AND nonJSON's content type IS msgpack
77	// (the alias never claims agreement for an unrelated non-JSON codec).
78	//
79	// An empty body never mismatches: it is not a valid non-JSON envelope
80	// regardless of what the header claims.
81	//
82	// A Client with no distinct non-JSON codec configured (nonJSON is the
83	// jsonrpc.JSONCodec{} default) never mismatches either: with nothing but
84	// JSON to disagree with, an ordinary JSON reply's own "Content-Type:
85	// application/json" header would otherwise satisfy headerSaysNonJSON's
86	// literal string comparison against nonJSON.ContentType() (also
87	// "application/json"), producing a false-positive mismatch on every
88	// zero-config JSON call — a bug this guard forecloses rather than lets a
89	// caller's mismatch check ever observe.
90	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
91	```
92	
93	## The verdicts
94	
95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |
102	| `trimUTF8BOM` | 6 lines | DELETE | the name is the documentation; the encoding/json quirk belongs to `replyBytesForDecode`, its only decode-side caller |
103	| `detectReplyCodec` | 7 lines | DELETE | narrated implementation ("Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice") plus cross-repo provenance |
104	| `replyBytesForDecode` | 8 lines | one-liner survives | an external library quirk: encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading byte, not whitespace |
105	| `normalizeContentType` | 4 lines | DELETE | the name says it; the caller list rots |
106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |
107	| `replyCodecAndMismatch` | 22 lines | one-liner survives | the package's one real policy: bytes pick the decoder, the header is only a signal — the rest moves to the feature doc |
108	
109	Four one-liners survive out of nine comments; roughly 68 comment lines become 4.
110	
111	## The after
112	
113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```
194	
195	The knowledge that was worth keeping and did not fit a one-liner — the
196	msgpack-alias carve-out, why a JSON-only client never reports a mismatch — moves
197	to the feature doc, where the exported caller's godoc points with its See-edge.
198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.
200	
201	## The lesson
202	
203	The tier budget caps how big a comment can be; only the visibility default
204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"
205	read as permission, and a writer in fill-the-menu mode gave every private symbol
206	its tier maximum — nine comments, each locally justified, jointly unreadable.
207	The default for unexported symbols is **zero**: the name is the documentation,
208	and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first. The
209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package
213	doc, or the feature doc.

You are the overabstraction-skeptic: a read-only devil's advocate. Your job is to try to KILL each proposed type/interface extraction below. Every refutation MUST propose a cheaper alternative — never just "no". Score each with R1's juiciness scorecard.

PAYLOAD 1 — R1's Juiciness scoring and over-abstraction trap (verbatim):
=====
### Juiciness scoring

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type.
=====

PAYLOAD 2 — the CIDR over-abstraction case file (verbatim, your case law):
=====
# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function, two booleans tracked related
state. Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win. The trap
appeared one step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
type CIDRPresence bool
func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool { return bool(p) } // just unwraps!
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. 8 lines of code for a trivial wrapper.
2. One method that just unwraps.
3. No type safety gained — still just a bool underneath.
4. Not more readable — compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` with `config.ClusterCIDRSet`.
5. No validation, no logic, no invariants — pure ceremony. Scores 0-1 on R1's scorecard.
6. Increases cognitive load for nothing.

The rejection identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: controlled
mutation. Naming the actual need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
`ClusterCIDRSet bool` reads exactly as well as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at zero
ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern.

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}
func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
```

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled.

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**
Rejecting a wrapper was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need at lower cost. A bare "don't create the type" would have left
the original defect in place. The skeptic's job is two moves, always together: name
the need the proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming
when the need is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled
mutation, and a real type only when the need is validation or behavior.
=====

=====
### Juiciness scoring

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type.

# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function, two booleans tracked related
state. Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win. The trap
appeared one step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
type CIDRPresence bool
func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool { return bool(p) } // just unwraps!
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. 8 lines of code for a trivial wrapper.
2. One method that just unwraps.
3. No type safety gained — still just a bool underneath.
4. Not more readable — compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` with `config.ClusterCIDRSet`.
5. No validation, no logic, no invariants — pure ceremony. Scores 0-1 on R1's scorecard.
6. Increases cognitive load for nothing.

The rejection identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: controlled
mutation. Naming the actual need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
`ClusterCIDRSet bool` reads exactly as well as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at zero
ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern.

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}
func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
```

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled.

You are the comment-critic: a read-only adversarial reviewer whose single obsession is comment value. Judge every comment in the DIFF SCOPE against the three-test standard below. Every non-KEEP verdict must name the toolbox item the replacement should deliver.

PAYLOAD 1 — R9's comment policy section (verbatim):
=====
### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2).

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values: WHY not WHAT — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot
carry; Wider context — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it;
Important use cases / flows — when to reach for it; Boundary contract — dos/don'ts,
valid inputs, error behavior; Guarantees — thread safety, nil handling, invariants;
Network edge — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain.

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3)
must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table") — **restated
     repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo already applies
     everywhere — and **provenance and decoder-ring references** — PR numbers,
     review items, plan/decision/test-plan IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement
     tags, spec section refs, "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what
     <old system> did". The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five
     years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round
     produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense rationale, and an
     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
     constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget.
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists,
   stacked clauses, academic phrasing, unexplained acronyms or insider jargon.
   Second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be understandable BEFORE
   reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or another comment — to
   understand this comment, it has negative value.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free: blank `//` separator
lines; the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own
trailing line; short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines.

**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor (ParsePolicy, ParsePort), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** An unexported
function, type, constant, or variable defaults to **zero** comment lines: the
name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an
extraction first (R3-storifying). The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — an ordering requirement, an external library quirk,
the WHY of a magic number, the package's one real policy. If a private symbol
seems to need more than that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported
symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

Boundary with R3-storifying: block comments *inside* function bodies are R3's
(each is an extraction candidate — the fix is a function named after the
comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this rule's (they must carry
why/context, not restate the identifier).
=====

PAYLOAD 2 — Comment Value Toolbox catalog (verbatim):
=====
Each entry: when it earns its place, and what it looks like.

### WHY, not WHAT
Rationale, incident, or constraint the code cannot carry. The default value.
❌ ParseAddress parses an address string.  ✅ ParseAddress rejects ports below 1024: the collector runs unprivileged.

### Wider context
Where this sits architecturally; what depends on it.
❌ Queue is a queue used by the system.  ✅ Every exporter ships through this queue — backpressure starts here.

### Important use cases / flows
When to reach for this symbol instead of its neighbors.
✅ Use Snapshot for reads during a rebalance; direct reads block until it ends.

### Boundary contract
Dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior.
✅ Accepts "3x100ms"-style specs. Zero attempts and negative delays are rejected.

### Guarantees
Thread safety, nil handling, invariants.
✅ Safe for concurrent use; callbacks run outside the lock.

### Network edge
The `See docs/<feature>.md` line. Free under the budget.
✅ See docs/retry-policy.md for the incident and the cap math.

### What never earns a line: provenance and decoder-ring references
PR numbers, review items, plan/decision IDs ("T-04-02"), spec section refs. The
5-year reader test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW,
never which PR or review round produced it.

A comment justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere.

### What never earns a line: review-defense narration
The writer arguing with an imagined reviewer.
❌ Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice.
❌ This was discussed once and it was decided that the coupling is acceptable.

### The visibility default: private symbols get no comment
An unexported symbol defaults to zero comment lines; its name is the
documentation. Special case: one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.

     everywhere — and **provenance and decoder-ring references** — PR numbers,
     review items, plan/decision/test-plan IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement
     tags, spec section refs, "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what
     <old system> did". The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five
     years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round
     produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense rationale, and an
     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
     constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget.
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists,
   stacked clauses, academic phrasing, unexplained acronyms or insider jargon.
   Second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be understandable BEFORE
   reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or another comment — to
   understand this comment, it has negative value.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free: blank `//` separator
lines; the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own
trailing line; short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines.

**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor (ParsePolicy, ParsePort), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** An unexported
function, type, constant, or variable defaults to **zero** comment lines: the
name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an
extraction first (R3-storifying). The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — an ordering requirement, an external library quirk,
the WHY of a magic number, the package's one real policy. If a private symbol
seems to need more than that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported
symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

Boundary with R3-storifying: block comments *inside* function bodies are R3's
(each is an extraction candidate — the fix is a function named after the
comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this rule's (they must carry
why/context, not restate the identifier).
=====

PAYLOAD 2 — Comment Value Toolbox catalog (verbatim):
=====
Each entry: when it earns its place, and what it looks like.

### WHY, not WHAT
Rationale, incident, or constraint the code cannot carry. The default value.
❌ ParseAddress parses an address string.  ✅ ParseAddress rejects ports below 1024: the collector runs unprivileged.

### Wider context
Where this sits architecturally; what depends on it.
❌ Queue is a queue used by the system.  ✅ Every exporter ships through this queue — backpressure starts here.

### Important use cases / flows
When to reach for this symbol instead of its neighbors.
✅ Use Snapshot for reads during a rebalance; direct reads block until it ends.

### Boundary contract
Dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior.
✅ Accepts "3x100ms"-style specs. Zero attempts and negative delays are rejected.

### Guarantees
Thread safety, nil handling, invariants.
✅ Safe for concurrent use; callbacks run outside the lock.

### Network edge
The `See docs/<feature>.md` line. Free under the budget.
✅ See docs/retry-policy.md for the incident and the cap math.

### What never earns a line: provenance and decoder-ring references
PR numbers, review items, plan/decision IDs ("T-04-02"), spec section refs. The
5-year reader test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW,
never which PR or review round produced it.
❌ added in PR #87 after the outage; see T-04-02

### What never earns a line: restated repo idiom
A comment justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere.

### What never earns a line: review-defense narration
The writer arguing with an imagined reviewer.
❌ Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice.
❌ This was discussed once and it was decided that the coupling is acceptable.

### The visibility default: private symbols get no comment
An unexported symbol defaults to zero comment lines; its name is the
documentation. Special case: one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.

PAYLOAD 1 — R1's Juiciness scoring and over-abstraction trap (verbatim):
=====
### Juiciness scoring

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type.
=====

PAYLOAD 2 — the CIDR over-abstraction case file (verbatim, your case law):
=====
# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function, two booleans tracked related
state. Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win. The trap
appeared one step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
type CIDRPresence bool
func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool { return bool(p) } // just unwraps!
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. 8 lines of code for a trivial wrapper.
2. One method that just unwraps.
3. No type safety gained — still just a bool underneath.
4. Not more readable — compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` with `config.ClusterCIDRSet`.
5. No validation, no logic, no invariants — pure ceremony. Scores 0-1 on R1's scorecard.
6. Increases cognitive load for nothing.

The rejection identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: controlled
mutation. Naming the actual need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
`ClusterCIDRSet bool` reads exactly as well as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at zero
ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern.

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}
func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
```

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled.

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**
Rejecting a wrapper was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need at lower cost. A bare "don't create the type" would have left
the original defect in place. The skeptic's job is two moves, always together: name
the need the proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming
when the need is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled
mutation, and a real type only when the need is validation or behavior.
=====

that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2).

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values: WHY not WHAT — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot
carry; Wider context — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it;
Important use cases / flows — when to reach for it; Boundary contract — dos/don'ts,
valid inputs, error behavior; Guarantees — thread safety, nil handling, invariants;
Network edge — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain.

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3)
must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table") — **restated
     repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo already applies
     everywhere — and **provenance and decoder-ring references** — PR numbers,
     review items, plan/decision/test-plan IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement
     tags, spec section refs, "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what
     <old system> did". The floor's lens is the 5-year reader test: a reader five
     years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which PR or review round
     produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense rationale, and an
     incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the rationale for a
     constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the
     highest-value toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget.
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary where a common word exists,
   stacked clauses, academic phrasing, unexplained acronyms or insider jargon.
   Second half, **self-standing**: the comment must be understandable BEFORE
   reading the code. If the reader must read the code — or another comment — to
   understand this comment, it has negative value.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; these are free: blank `//` separator
lines; the `See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line — free ONLY as its own
trailing line; short inline example lines, bounded at 2–4 lines.

**Role-based tiers** — judge the tier from the symbol's role in the code:

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary; tiny example only if it clarifies |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor (ParsePolicy, ParsePort), self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract; dos/don'ts example (free) |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** An unexported
function, type, constant, or variable defaults to **zero** comment lines: the
name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an
extraction first (R3-storifying). The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — an ordering requirement, an external library quirk,
the WHY of a magic number, the package's one real policy. If a private symbol
seems to need more than that one line, the knowledge belongs to the exported
symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

Boundary with R3-storifying: block comments *inside* function bodies are R3's
(each is an extraction candidate — the fix is a function named after the
comment); doc comments *on* exported symbols are this rule's (they must carry
why/context, not restate the identifier).
